name: Evidence summary: DNA pathogen identification workflows
description: Plain-language summary of what the reviewed evidence shows. Draft until reviewed.

attributes.value: Most workflow comparisons in the reviewed evidence use mock communities, constructed metagenomes or simulated sequences. Two compare workflows on patient specimens, and in both the reference standard draws partly on sequencing: in Hu et al. 2026 only the culture comparison is independent of the sequencing results, and in Huang et al. 2026 the reference was built mainly from BALF mNGS and the conventional tests that are themselves scored. Both are author-reported and have co-authors from sequencing companies (Genskey Medical Technology for Hu; Geneplus-Beijing, which supplies the targeted assay's probes, for Huang). For the Karius plasma cell-free DNA assay, the developers report 93.7% (59 of 63) agreement with initial blood culture in a sepsis-alert cohort, and blood culture does not detect every infection. A prospective study in children and young adults with high-risk leukaemia, with Karius taking part in sample processing and analysis, found every blood-culture organism in 81.3% (65 of 80) of evaluable bloodstream infection episodes on the day of or after onset and in 51.9% (42 of 81) during the three days before; 82.7% (134 of 162) of control samples from patients without fever or infection had no bacterium or yeast detected. In 62 bronchoalveolar lavage specimens (Hu et al. 2026), a short-read MGI workflow and a host-depleted nanopore workflow both had 95.2% positive agreement with culture but 44.6% and 46.4% negative agreement, because they found organisms culture did not; against a composite reference that adds organisms found by both workflows, positive agreement was 93.3% and 90.7%. In 122 intensive-care patients with pneumonia-associated sepsis (Huang et al. 2026), a targeted probe-capture assay on plasma had 63.46% sensitivity against the reference diagnosis, against 35.58% for untargeted blood mNGS, 49.04% for conventional tests and 9.62% for blood culture, with specificity of 44.44% and 61.11% for the two blood sequencing assays. In mock communities (Portik et al. 2022), Kraken2 and Bracken called 44 to 204 absent species at a 0.001% read threshold (precision 0.05 to 0.21), while long-read MEGAN-LR and BugSeq-V2 called 0 to 2; the first author is a PacBio employee. In seven pathogen-free libraries scored against one shared virus database by the EsViritu developers (preprint), the median number of false virus species was 0 for EsViritu, Centrifuger and Sylph, 6 for Kraken2 and 18 for Metabuli. For M. tuberculosis reads in constructed metagenomes (Hall and Coin 2024), kraken with its standard database classified 0.07 to 0.74 of the M. tuberculosis reads as M. tuberculosis, against 0.97 to 0.995 with a Mycobacterium database. Two papers by the developers of trained classifiers compare them with the baseline tools, on simulated or isolate-derived data rather than clinical specimens. On simulated 1,500-nt genome fragments (Mock et al. 2022, BERTax), Kraken2 and minimap2 assigned a superkingdom to 76.11% and 75.59% of fragments, with 99.82% and 99.95% accuracy on the fragments they assigned, when relatives were in the reference, and to 21.56% and 19.88% with 90.71% and 94.42% accuracy when each fragment's genus was absent from it; BERTax assigned every fragment, with 94.78% and 88.95% accuracy in the two settings. On in silico mixtures of nanopore isolate reads from species absent from the reference (Peres da Silva et al. 2024, MetageNN), MetageNN assigned a genus to 93.26% of reads on average across 30 mixtures, against 64.90% for Kraken2 and 53.06% for MEGAN-LR (on minimap2 alignments); MMseqs2, a reference-based tool not in the baseline, assigned 85.49%. These shares count reads assigned, not reads assigned correctly. Each study used its own reference database and reporting rules, and none of these results is clinical validation.

attributes.value: The five sources whose comparisons are shown on this page score how well models predict expression changes after genetic perturbations they were not trained on. Each uses its own split, gene set and metric, so their values are not pooled. Ahlmann-Eltze et al. 2025, who did not develop the deep models and ran them all themselves, scored held-out two-gene CRISPRa perturbations in K562 cells (Norman), training on every single-gene perturbation and half of the pairs. A baseline that adds the two single-gene effects had a mean L2 distance of 2.766 and a Pearson delta of 0.892 over the 1,000 most highly expressed genes, against 3.478 and 0.773 for Geneformer with a linear decoder, 4.096 and 0.631 for GEARS, 4.279 and 0.610 for both UCE and scBERT, 4.616 and 0.527 for scGPT, 4.722 and 0.537 for scFoundation, and 12.205 and 0.146 for CPA; predicting no change gave an L2 distance of 5.616. Rewire computed these means from the authors' Source Data, no spread is stated, and the UCE and scBERT runs used ground-truth expression of the perturbed genes, a possible test leakage. In PerturBench v4, a preprint whose authors trained every model and built the Linear, Latent Additive and Decoder baselines, the cosine similarity of predicted log fold change on held-out Norman pairs ranged from 0.41 for Biolord and 0.44 for GEARS to 0.79 for the Latent Additive baseline, with CPA at 0.76 and the Linear baseline at 0.60, each a mean over five training seeds. When effects were transferred to melanoma co-culture (Frangieh21) every model scored between 0.01 and 0.22 and every printed DEG recall was 0.000; on held-out cell line and cytokine states (Jiang24) scores ranged from 0.17 for Linear to 0.64 for the Decoder baseline, and the paper describes the held-out states in two different ways. In Csendes et al. 2025, whose authors are employees of Turbine Ltd. and built the baselines themselves, predicting the mean training response gave a higher Pearson delta than scGPT and scFoundation, as re-run by the same authors, on all four Perturb-seq datasets: 0.711, 0.557, 0.373 and 0.628 for Adamson, Norman, Replogle K562 and Replogle RPE1, against 0.641, 0.554, 0.327 and 0.596 for scGPT and 0.552, 0.459, 0.269 and 0.471 for scFoundation. Each dataset there has one split and one run per model with no spread printed, so small gaps such as 0.557 against 0.554 cannot be tested. The GEARS developers report a mean squared error of 0.216 for GEARS on Norman, against 0.354 for CPA and 0.551 for a no-change control, with spreads of unstated type. PertEval-scFM, whose authors trained GEARS from scratch, reports an area under its distribution-shift curve of 0.815 for GEARS against 4.484 for an MLP and 4.612 for a mean baseline, lower being better. All of these scores measure agreement with observed expression in held-out perturbations; they do not show which experiments will succeed.
